- Single-panel chart
- Horizontal category layout by product type
- Two dots per category connected by a light gray line
- Color used to distinguish the two comparison groups
- No faceting or small multiples
- Not stacked

| Change in price (%) | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |

| Time period (January 2019 to October 2023) | Temporal | Shown in title/context, applying to all plotted values |

The first thing I notice while looking at the graph is that basic household items are increasing in price significantly.I also notice that the time period is from 2019-2023, where a large amount of inflation has occurred. raw_comment: This graph examines the effects of inflation, especially after the global pandemic that occurred in 2020. The graph shows how much more expensive items were at the end of 2023 as compared to the beginning of 2019. A lot of this price change is due to the COVID-19 pandemic which led to a lot of scarcity and overshopping from people across the globe. I think an important piece of evidence to support this is the most inflated item is household paper items, the things that were most in demand during the pandemic (toilet paper, paper towels, tissues, etc). I think this graph is focused on the United States because its source is the Bureau of Labor Statistics, a US government branch. I also was interested in the accounting for size portion of this graph, because my family and I always notice how products seem to be getting smaller while prices stay the same, or even grow. This graph is proof of our experience. I would title this graph: "More Bang For Your Buck? Not in 2023!"

These items include coffee, household cleaning products, snacks, candy and chewing gum, and household paper products. Every single product listed has gone up in price in those recent years, with paper products being the most and coffee increasing the least. I wonder why everything is increasing, and if it has to do with the COVID outbreaks or the inflation that has been clear recently. Some of these products since COVID have been more needed by everyone. This relates to me because I am a user of many of these products who also has paid the different rising prices for these products in the last 5 years. 

My headline is: Predicting the Prices

image_description:
1. **Chart type**: Dumbbell chart (connected dot plot / slope-style comparison chart).

2. **Layout techniques**:
- Single-panel chart
- Horizontal category layout by product type
- Two dots per category connected by a light gray line
- Color used to distinguish the two comparison groups
- No faceting or small multiples
- Not stacked

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Product category (Coffee; Household cleaning products; Snacks; Candy and chewing gum; Household paper products) | Categorical/nominal | Position on y-axis; text labels |
| Change in price (%) | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Adjustment status / comparison group (“Not accounting for size” vs “Accounting for size”) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of dots; top text labels indicating color meaning |
| Time period (January 2019 to October 2023) | Temporal | Shown in title/context, applying to all plotted values |

Thanks to all the students who responded.   Here are some of the catchy headlines that we received: “A Closer Look at the Price and Size of Consumer Items!” by Kemoura from Perth Amboy High School in New Jersey, “How Does Size Influence Price?" Trey of Elk Rapids High School in Mich. , “Shrinkage Increases Inflation” by GCA in SoCal, and four headlines from California Polytechnic State University, San Luis Obispo:  “How Hidden Changes in Product Size Impact Your Wallet” by Kylie; “Size Matters: Unpacking Grocery Store Price Hikes” by Isabelle; "Secret Shrinkage: Tracking Hidden Risings in Grocery Bills" by Hailey and "’Shrink-flation’: Less Product for Your Dollar" by Alexander.

The next graph will be released by Friday, April 19 with live-moderation two-weeks later on Wednesday, May 1.  The topic is still to be determined.
 
Signing off – Sharon Hessney from Boston, who is missing the half-quart from the half-gallon of ice cream, and Tonya Adkins of Charlotte, N.C., who recently had a related conversation regarding Reece’s Cups!

All the items in the graph had at least a +20% increase in price, with household paper products going above +30% and coffee having the least increase. Shrinkflation Shown In A Graph

When the demand is high and the supply is low, it is inevitable for prices to go up. Although coffee has increased the least in price out of all the products listed, the price has still increased significantly and it is noticeable. I constantly hear my dad complaining about coffee prices. Additionally, the price of snacks and candy at my school has gone up 50 cents in this past year. This makes me less likely to want to buy snacks from school because I would rather save my money and not buy expensive snacks/candy. I wonder if this is true for the global market. Are sales of these items declining because of how inflated the prices are?

1. **Chart type**: Dumbbell chart (connected dot plot / slope-style comparison chart).

2. **Layout techniques**:
- Single-panel chart
- Horizontal category layout by product type
- Two dots per category connected by a light gray line
- Color used to distinguish the two comparison groups
- No faceting or small multiples
- Not stacked

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Product category (Coffee; Household cleaning products; Snacks; Candy and chewing gum; Household paper products) | Categorical/nominal | Position on y-axis; text labels |
| Change in price (%) | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Adjustment status / comparison group (“Not accounting for size” vs “Accounting for size”) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of dots; top text labels indicating color meaning |
| Time period (January 2019 to October 2023) | Temporal | Shown in title/context, applying to all plotted values |
raw_comment:
This graph depicts the rise in prices for common grocery items, such as snacks or cleaning products, from January 2019 to October 2023. The graph accounts for with and without size/weight of each item. All of these items have surpassed a 20% increase. Household paper products, when accounting for size, have the largest increase on this graph with a surge of 35%. The smallest price increase, which is just over 20%, is coffee (not accounting for size). What stuck out to me the most is that candy and gum, when accounting for size, have an almost 30% increase as compared to cleaning products with less than a 25% increase. I wonder why candy increased more than other products. I wonder what this graph would look like if more items. For example, if meats, bread, and dairy were accounted for. Would they have price increases too? I also wonder if this graph would be affected by data from November 2023 to now. Would there be any significant changes? This affects my community because the price of living increases with every year. As a student entering college soon, having to worry about college expenses as well as everyday things I may need, such as food and cleaning supplies, will be difficult. Both expenses are becoming more expensive every day. All students my age are worried about affordability as we take our next steps into adulthood. Will we be able to live in a world where buying gum is becoming too expensive?

“Are These Prices Eating You? Food Prices Jump Since January 2019”

raw_comment:
I notice that household paper products have the largest increase in price (+31-35%) from January 2019 to October 2023. I also notice that coffee has increased in price the least (+20.5-23%). Interestingly, the change in price when accounting for size is consistently larger than when not accounting for size. 

I wonder why the price of household paper products has increased. During the pandemic, many people were obsessed with the toilet paper shortage, increasing demand. I wonder if this demand led manufacturers to increase prices. I also wonder if environmental factors, such as lumber shortages, affects the price of paper. I wonder if the change in price accounting for size is larger than not accounting for size because less product is being sold. I am curious if the trend of increased prices is also caused by inflation.

This affects me an my community because we purchase these goods at inflated prices. Paper and household cleaning products are perhaps the most functional, but all can be enjoyed day-to-day. People may have to limit their superfluous purchases (such as candy and snacks) in the future if prices continue to rise.

"Cheap Grocery Runs: A Post-Pandemic Casualty?"

raw_comment:
The first thing that stood out to me was the large increase in the prices of household items, especially when looking at the increase after accounting for size. The large increase accounting for size is interesting to me, since it implies that the products being sold today are simultaneously more expensive and less efficient per unit. I wonder how much of these price raises were caused by the Covid pandemic and then never decreased once things went back to the new normal. For a lot of the lower cost items, such as the coffee and the candy, the percent change doesn't change the total price that much, but there is still the trend of companies charging more while offering less overall. I wonder if these trends also appear in general groceries and other everyday products, and  also how these changes in general compare to changes in wage and cost of living. Knowing how prices of products have changed can help inform large scale wage changes on local, state, and federal level. In order for wages to be adjusted in a way that properly reflects the cost of everyday life, you need to have a complete knowledge of the factors going into that cost.
A title for the graph could be "Less Bang for your Buck: Shrinkflation in Today's Economy"

raw_comment:
What do you notice?

I've noticed that the prices of the five common grocery items have increased by at least 20% in the last four years, with the smallest increase seen in coffee and the largest in household paper products. Along with having the highest increase when size is not accounted for, household paper products also achieved a higher rate of increase when size is accounted for.

- What do you wonder?

I wonder if the gray lines in between the blue and orange dots signify some sort of continuous relationship between percent change and size or if it simply connects the two dots.  

Although inflation is expected for many products, I also wonder why candy and chewing gum ranked second in the highest increase and why household cleaning products did not increase as much as household paper products. 

- How does this relate to you and your community?

As a student, it is important to understand inflation as we are starting to learn to budget. Understanding the causes of inflation and its consequences will help us with long-term financial planning.

- Catchy headline

Your Grocery Bill Just Got Bigger

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that the prices for all categories have increased over time. Not only that, but the increase is more pronounced when size is not accounted for, indicating that size or quantity reductions (hello, shrinkflation!) are masking some of the price increases.
2. This makes me really curious about how more perishable grocery items have increased in price or decreased in size, based on what we are observing with more shelf stable items. It also makes me wonder how these changes in quantity/size impact overall cost of living.
3. As college students, these questions are especially relevant. For those of us getting by with grants and scholarships, we have a fixed amount of money each term that has to cover tuition, books, and our living expenses. When we have to pay more for the same quantity, or the same for a smaller quantity of a necessary item, our money doesn’t take us as far, necessitating part time work at the expense of internships or research. 
4. Based on this, I think that “Size Matters: Unpacking Grocery Store Price Hikes” would be an apt title.

raw_comment: The first thing I noticed was how much each product’s price change increased when accounting for quantity and size, nodding to how companies are increasing prices because of inflation but also decreasing the quantity/volume of products to reach desirable profit margins. Given that consumers purchase these products very often, it is probably difficult to notice subtle changes in quantity especially over long periods. I wonder whether this trend applies to all other consumer items since there could be other items that may not be as different when, for example, adjusting for size or increasing prices due to inflation. I also wonder how household paper products' largest change in price relates to COVID-19 when many households stocked up on toilet paper to the point where stores ran out of paper products. I wonder if these household paper product companies noticed how crucial their products are to consumers and decided to increase profit margins even greater than they were before. This relates to me both as a consumer and a statistician because, in an economy already struggling with inflation, shrinkflation, COVID-19 recovery, etc., it is difficult to navigate what products are worth my time and money. To see these companies increasing their profit margins makes me question whether they have their consumers’ best interests in mind or solely want to exploit us for money. A catchy headline could be “Pockets Feeling Lighter? Higher Prices and Lesser Quantities Could Explain Why.”

1. **Chart type**: Dumbbell chart (connected dot plot / slope-style comparison chart).

2. **Layout techniques**:
- Single-panel chart
- Horizontal category layout by product type
- Two dots per category connected by a light gray line
- Color used to distinguish the two comparison groups
- No faceting or small multiples
- Not stacked

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Product category (Coffee; Household cleaning products; Snacks; Candy and chewing gum; Household paper products) | Categorical/nominal | Position on y-axis; text labels |
| Change in price (%) | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Adjustment status / comparison group (“Not accounting for size” vs “Accounting for size”) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of dots; top text labels indicating color meaning |
| Time period (January 2019 to October 2023) | Temporal | Shown in title/context, applying to all plotted values |
raw_comment:
The first thing I noticed is the scale of the x-axis. First of all, since the x-axis does not start at 0, the price increase of coffee seems to be small in comparison to the others, even though a 20% increase is still fairly large. Additionally, since the x-axis is based on percentage increases instead of actual dollar increases, it standardizes the scale so it is easier to compare the 5 items. However, this means we do not know how the dollars increased, so it can be difficult to interpret the actual difference in pricing. Since the item categories are very general, I wonder what items are included in each category, and how the prices are calculated across all those items. This information is very relevant to everyone in my community because we all went through the pandemic, so to see how most of the products being used on a daily basis have increased significantly from before coronavirus hit the US is quite important to us all. Also, as a college student, knowing how much more these items are costing motivates me to save more and reduce my spending on unnecessary items.
Title:  “Less Costs More: How Shrinkflation is Affecting Essentials Post-Pandemic”

This sure leaves you with something to think about. 🤔

raw_comment:
When looking at the graph I notice that for every one of the five popular grocery store items, when size is accounted for the change in price for all items goes up by a higher percentage. I also notice that this graph includes pre, mid, and post pandemic dates which would be an influence in the price fluctuations. I think that the grocery stores have found that because these are such staple household items, they can easily raise prices and cover that with size without the consumers noticing.

I wonder if the reason in the increase is due to inflation. I know these past few years inflation rates have been at an all time high and that could definitely be a reason for the price increase. I also am wondering if maybe the demand of COVID and the fact that during the pandemic most of these items were hard to come by, especially paper products, has allowed grocery stores to raise their prices without the consequence of less people buying them. And the fact that they were able to raise the prices has given them confidence to constantly keep increasing the prices of these items.

This directly applies to my community of being a student in college who does not have a full time job nor steady income. These items are ones that I know both me and many of my peers purchase almost weekly. The increase in prices makes these essential items less affordable but because of the constant demand, prices will not drop and we are forced to pay it.

- Horizontal category layout by product type
- Two dots per category connected by a light gray line
- Color used to distinguish the two comparison groups
- No faceting or small multiples
- Not stacked

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Product category (Coffee; Household cleaning products; Snacks; Candy and chewing gum; Household paper products) | Categorical/nominal | Position on y-axis; text labels |
| Change in price (%) | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |

raw_comment:
I notice that accounting for the change in size when considering the percent change in price for all 5 grocery items makes the change more significant. The companies likely try to influence consumers to believe the price changes are not very much by not accounting for the accompanying change in size. In reality, this change in size can have a substantial effect on the value consumers are receiving for their money. 

I wonder the extent to which the public is aware of these tactics. Are most consumers cognizant of the relationship between price changes and accompanying changes in product size? I know that for me, I feel deceived after looking at this graph. I had not considered the effect of the change in size on the true change in the price of a product. I wonder if others feel similarly or if they already knew about this and accepted it. 

In my community, I believe this discussion could spark a range of insights and reflections. Discussions within the community could also delve into potential solutions or responses to these practices. Members might brainstorm ideas for promoting greater transparency in pricing or advocating for stronger consumer protections. 

Headline idea: How Hidden Changes in Product Size Impact Your Wallet
